description: Curated claims about cannabinoid oncology research. This is a distinct biological-activity and clinical-context ledger, not phytocannabinoid identification or treatment advice.
editorial_notice: This first release summarizes a 2016 mechanistic review and the National Cancer Institute's living PDQ professional summary as consulted in October 2026. It is not a systematic review, practice guideline, efficacy assessment, or clinical prescribing resource.
medical_boundary: Cannabinoids are not established anticancer treatments in humans. Preclinical findings must not be interpreted as clinical efficacy. Cancer patients should discuss cannabinoid use, including potential interactions, with their oncology team.

sources.title: Anticancer mechanisms of cannabinoids
sources.authors: Velasco G, Sánchez C, Guzmán M
sources.note: Reviews preclinical cell and animal studies, resistance mechanisms, and early human feasibility studies; secondary synthesis, not a primary assay receipt.

sources.title: Cannabis and Cannabinoids (PDQ®) – Health Professional Version
sources.note: Living source; findings here reflect the summary consulted on 2026-10-25, and may change after this release.

claims.title: THC-associated stress signaling and cell death in glioma models
claims.model: Cell culture and animal models, chiefly glioma
claims.summary: The 2016 review describes cannabinoid-receptor-associated ceramide production, ER stress, NUPR1/ATF4/CHOP/TRIB3 signaling, inhibition of AKT/mTORC1, and autophagy upstream of apoptosis in experimental glioma systems.
mechanism_steps: Autophagy-associated apoptosis observed in some models
claims.boundary: A mechanistic model of selected experimental systems, not proof of tumor clearance, selective safety, or patient benefit.

claims.title: CBD-associated cancer-cell responses in experimental systems
claims.model: Cell culture and animal studies across selected tumor models
claims.summary: The 2016 review discusses CBD-associated cell death and reduced invasiveness in selected experimental models, proposing reactive-oxygen-species and TRPV2-related routes that may act independently of CB1/CB2.
mechanism_steps: CBD exposure in selected preclinical models
Proposed ROS or TRPV2-associated signaling, depending on model
Altered cell survival or invasiveness observed experimentally
claims.boundary: Proposed mechanisms and model-dependent results; not established clinical anticancer efficacy and not a universal CBD effect.

claims.title: Angiogenesis and invasion findings in some preclinical tumors
claims.summary: The review discusses decreased VEGF-pathway signaling, invasion, or metastasis in some cannabinoid-treated experimental tumor systems, with different pathways reported for different compounds and cancers.
mechanism_steps: Model-dependent VEGF signaling or invasion-related changes
Reduced angiogenesis or invasion in certain animal/cell experiments
claims.boundary: Preclinical observations do not demonstrate prevention of metastasis or improved survival in humans.

claims.title: Potential tumor-promoting or immune-suppressive contexts
claims.summary: The 2016 review explicitly describes conflicting findings: in some models cannabinoid-receptor stimulation may suppress antitumor immune surveillance or favor tumor progression, while other models show antitumor effects.
claims.boundary: Direction depends on cell type, immune context, compound, and conditions; do not represent cannabinoids as universally antitumor.

claims.title: Nine-person recurrent-glioblastoma THC pilot was not an efficacy trial
claims.model: Nine patients with recurrent glioblastoma; early phase I pilot reported in the 2016 review
claims.summary: The reviewed pilot administered THC intracranially and investigated feasibility, tolerability and exploratory tumor measures; nine participants cannot establish anticancer efficacy.
claims.boundary: Human pilot feasibility must not be promoted to proof of effectiveness, a recommended route, or a treatment protocol.

claims.title: Cancer-related symptom support is distinct from treating cancer
claims.model: Clinical research and NCI clinical evidence summary
claims.summary: NCI distinguishes use of cannabinoid medicines, including dronabinol and nabilone for certain chemotherapy-related nausea and vomiting, from unproven claims that cannabis treats the cancer itself.
claims.boundary: Approved or studied symptom-relief indications do not establish anticancer effects; drug products are not interchangeable with unstandardized cannabis.

claims.title: No established human anticancer efficacy
claims.model: Human clinical evidence as characterized in the NCI summary
claims.summary: The NCI evidence summary does not establish cannabis or cannabinoids as effective antineoplastic treatment in humans; potential interactions and safety issues require clinical discussion.
claims.boundary: Do not substitute cannabis or cannabinoids for evidence-based cancer care, or use this research atlas to make treatment decisions.
